entities.name: Carnegie Mellon University
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), founded in 1900 by industrialist Andrew Carnegie as the Carnegie Technical Schools in Pittsburgh's Oakland neighborhood, is the world's leading computer science university — responsible for creating artificial intelligence as a formal discipline (with Simon and Newell's Logic Theorist, 1956), pioneering human-computer interaction (HCI), and producing a disproportionate share of Silicon Valley's technical leadership. CMU alumni and researchers founded or lead Google, Oracle, Intel, Lyft, and hundreds of other technology companies.

Andrew Carnegie founded the institution to provide practical technical education for Pittsburgh's working-class industrial families. The 1967 merger with the Mellon Institute of Industrial Research (funded by the Mellon banking family) created Carnegie Mellon University. Herbert Simon and Allen Newell's Logic Theorist (1956) — the first artificial intelligence program, demonstrated at Dartmouth Conference — was created at what is now CMU. The CMU Computer Science Department (established 1965) was the first separate computer science department at any university.

CMU's School of Computer Science encompasses multiple sub-fields that it pioneered: machine learning (with the first ML PhD program), robotics (the National Robotics Engineering Center), computational biology, human-computer interaction (the first HCI PhD program), and language technologies. CMU's autonomous vehicle research program — including the 1995 No Hands Across America demonstration (a car driving coast-to-coast with 98% autonomous control) — laid groundwork for self-driving vehicles. The Duolingo language learning app, used by 500 million people, was built on CMU language technology research.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Carnegie Mellon created the first AI program (Logic Theorist, 1956) and the first computer science department (1965), making it the founding institution of computer science as an academic discipline — the discipline that defined the 21st century's most consequential technologies.
